idiom_name: sealed interface/class + data class / data object cases + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: `sealed` restricts direct subclasses to the same package/module (sealed interfaces since 1.5), so the compiler knows the complete set and checks `when` for exhaustiveness; `data class`es (and `data object`s for nullary cases, stable since 1.9) supply value equality, `copy` and destructuring. A `when` used as an expression fails to compile when a case is missing, while the statement form only warns - the guarantee is bought by returning or assigning the result. The classic abstract-base-plus-visitor structure survives only when behaviour rather than data is the extension axis or when Java interop dictates it; otherwise sealed + data + when fully replaces it, with `sealed interface` preferred whenever a case must implement more than one hierarchy.
pitfalls: The restriction covers direct subclasses only: a non-sealed direct subclass can be extended anywhere its visibility allows, so cases should be `sealed`/`data`/`final` to keep the closure transitive.
A non-exhaustive `when` statement compiles with a warning; only the expression form breaks the build, so case analysis should be written as an expression rather than a statement.
A sealed *class* uses the single inheritance slot, so a case that must also implement another interface hierarchy needs a sealed interface instead.
`data class` properties are `val` but may reference mutable objects: a `MutableList` payload still changes under the case after construction.
